lesson.title: Global Variables: Names That Outlive Any Single Function
lesson.summary: A global variable is defined at the top level of a script, outside any function, and stays readable from anywhere in that file for as long as the program runs, unlike a local variable tied to one call.
lesson.body:
Local variables live and die with a single function call, confined to that call's own scope. Global variables are the opposite: any name assigned at the top level of a script, outside every function, belongs to the module's global scope, which exists for the entire run of the program and can be read from anywhere in that file, including from inside a function.

Reading a global variable from inside a function needs no special syntax at all. Consider:

tax_rate = 0.08

def total_with_tax(price):
    return price * (1 + tax_rate)

print(total_with_tax(100))

Here tax_rate is never defined inside total_with_tax's own local scope, so when the function needs its value, Python looks outward and finds it in the enclosing global scope instead. total_with_tax(100) computes 100 * (1 + 0.08), which is 108.0, and print displays 108.0. No parameter was needed to hand tax_rate to the function; being global made it visible without any extra work.

This automatic reading only goes one direction, and that is where global variables get subtle. If a function tries to assign to a name that shares a global variable's name, Python decides, for that entire function body, that the name is local, not global, even on lines that come before the assignment. Consider:

counter = 0

def increment():
    counter = counter + 1
    return counter

Calling increment() raises UnboundLocalError, cannot access local variable 'counter' where it is not associated with a value. Because counter is assigned somewhere inside the function, Python treats counter as local for the whole function, including on the right-hand side of counter + 1, where it tries to read a local counter that has not been given a value yet, and it never looks outward to the global counter = 0 at all.

This restriction applies specifically to assignment, not to mutating an object in place. If a global variable holds a mutable object like a list, a function can call methods on it, such as .append(), without triggering UnboundLocalError and without needing any special declaration, because no assignment to the name itself happens there, only a change to the object the name already points to. It is specifically writing counter = something inside the function body that makes Python treat counter as local for that entire function.

Fixing this properly requires the global keyword, covered next, which tells Python explicitly that an assignment inside the function should modify the outer variable rather than create a new local one. Until then, it is worth noting that relying heavily on global variables makes a program harder to reason about, since any function might depend on or quietly assume the current value of shared state; true constants like tax_rate, set once and only ever read, are a reasonable and common use, but variables that many functions modify are worth using sparingly.
